Minor changes.
"memfd" is an internal detail that shouldn't be exposed to users.  I think this is supposed to be a URI?

> I think this is supposed to be a URI?

I do not see how to construct a unique URI here, since no task has yet been created and i assume we discard the package on failure to discard the update.

message registry spec for `UpdateSkipped` says
```
2. string: The identifier for the image.
◦ This argument shall contain the identifier for the image
```

Now that `memfd` identifier is not unique so it does not `identify` anything.
Do you think it makes sense to compute the hash of the pldm package blob we receive?

That way we could refer to it, uniquely, without having to keep it around, but there may be some delay while computing the hash.

> > I think this is supposed to be a URI?
> 
> I do not see how to construct a unique URI here, since no task has yet been created and i assume we discard the package on failure to discard the update.
> 
> message registry spec for `UpdateSkipped` says
> ```
> 2. string: The identifier for the image.
> ◦ This argument shall contain the identifier for the image
> ```
> 
> Now that `memfd` identifier is not unique so it does not `identify` anything.

Yep, that's the problem.

> Do you think it makes sense to compute the hash of the pldm package blob we receive?

I don't really think so given that the hash doesn't actually mean anything.  Ideally the error message would contain enough information that we can construct a correct message.  Otherwise we should stick with the more generic error message.

> 
> That way we could refer to it, uniquely, without having to keep it around, but there may be some delay while computing the hash.

The message here is: "Message": "Device '%1' skipped the update with image '%2'.",

So presumably the second arg should be some kind of version information.

But the version information is inside the PLDM packgage, right?

So we do not have the version information here.

> Ideally the error message would contain enough information that we can construct a correct message. Otherwise we should stick with the more generic error message.

The intent is to give the redfish client some idea about what went wrong and to figure out if there is a temporary failure (update in progress), a fixable failure requiring change of update strategy (incorrect apply time) or an non-fixable failure if there is some issue with the update package itself.

That way an automated redfish update client can recover from some of these failures.

> I don't really think so given that the hash doesn't actually mean anything.

The hash allows the redfish client to map that back to whichever update package it sent. We just have to choose a hash algorithm for which there is a convenient cli tool to run it, so it works for interactive users as-well.


IMO the package hash is *identifying* the update package better than any version string since the version string can be the *same* even if the component image is different in the PLDM package.

What do you think?

> So we do not have the version information here.

That might be something to fix in PLDM?  Yes, differentiating errors is good.

A hash isn't really human readable, so it doesn't hit the intent.

Still "memfd" isn't something a user should be aware of, and isn't a correct construction of the error code.  If we need to extract more properties from the error to properly create the redfish, so be it.

> A hash isn't really human readable, so it doesn't hit the intent.

```
2. string: The identifier for the image.
◦ This argument shall contain the identifier for the image.
```

In case of `messages::verificationFailed` the pldm package could be corrupted, right?

In which case we cannot parse it.

Which implies we have no version string in that case.

Now, is it allowed to identify the package by different kinds of information in the different error messages?

That would mean the redfish client has to look up each error and based on that map back to which kind of identifying information is to be used.

> That might be something to fix in PLDM? Yes, differentiating errors is good.

The errors we get from fw update code do not have space for a custom message, at least not from what i have seen.

So there is no space to add any extra information there. bmcweb would have to parse the pldm package itself to extract a version string.

So we need some identifying information which everyone understands, and which works consistently in all error cases, which is the hash.

What if we made it 

`${hash}_${optional_version_string}`. 

That would allow clients to uniquely identify a file via the hash and then have optional version string later on in case
it is possible to do that in the future.

We can separate with underscore. So the automated redfish client would be able to deal with errors via the hash, without having to parse the pldm package.

And the optional version string could be shown to a human in case it's present.

IMO showing a fancy message could also be confusing to the user.

They may just be uploading a pldm package and not necessarily able to parse it due to lack of tool in their environment.

In which case showing any information from inside the package could actually be confusing to the user since they would not know what you are referring to.

If you say `"Device xyz skipped the update with image b2sum(0x1234abcd...)_v1.34"`
that is something someone may be able to map back to an actual file from logs alone.

If it's only some string from inside the package you are already assuming knowledge about PLDM from the user.

And then it gets confusing. Let's compare 2 messages
`"Device xyz skipped the update with image b2sum(0x1234abcd...)_v1.34"`
`"Device xyz skipped the update with image b2sum(0x9448abe7...)_v1.34"`

and 

`"Device xyz skipped the update with image v1.34"`
`"Device xyz skipped the update with image v1.34"`

so if we only show the version string, the message is no longer properly *identifying* the update package. We need the hash to do that.

What do you think? Is `b2sum` the right approach ?

https://www.blake2.net/

These are not decisions to be made by the webserver.  The point is that the identifier should not be hardcoded, and should be coming from the backend OR we should use a less specific message that doesn't require a human facing identifier.  The webserver should not be hardcoding arguments like "memfd".

The specific implementation of that belongs in a review for whatever backend you're using.


> And the optional version string could be shown to a human in case it's present.

This is kind of the point.  in the message you've used, this version string IS NOT optional.

What's your advice / requirement, how should it be done?
In line with the Redfish specification, without mention of internal details like "memfd"

Why updateInProgress over ServiceTemporarilyUnavailable which I think maps better to Common.Error.Unavailable?

I guess we mapped it to ResourceInUse at https://github.com/openbmc/bmcweb/blob/eb261e1f5455575234246764e73ef07d4a50031b/redfish-core/lib/log_services.hpp#L905

It means that an update is in progress. I tried to get a special error code for this purpose in

https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/+/82723/comment/5adb7705_8c50ebfd/

but got a review that

> This is already being done via Unavailable error code, so we don't need a new code here for InProgress.

IMO the "update in progress" scenario is meaningfully different from a service being unavailable since it could be unavailable due to other reason like power state transition or something else.

"update in progress" is a specific error condition which should ideally always go away in a *reasonable* amount of time.

It's the most specific error message i can think of that we can emit here.

I can go with `ServiceTemporarilyUnavailable` if it's required but i would prefer to have a more specific error.

> This is already being done via Unavailable error code, so we don't need a new code here for InProgress.

Where was that said?  i'm a little surprised we don't want to differentiate between those two cases.

> Where was that said?  i'm a little surprised we don't want to differentiate between those two cases.
